Well, the good news is that there are plenty of open-source agents that can be used locally (offline) on your own PC, allowing you to run models and agents directly on your own PC. To find the best open-source Windows agent for you, we’re going to look at five of the most popular and see what they offer. ## The Caveats of Local Before we get into the agents, it’s important to remember that local AI will still have other considerations. These include: * The need for maintenance and updates * Running through local LLMs * Taking up space on your machine as they learn * Integration with various tools ## A Good Open-Source Windows Agent – Our Choices Below, we’ve got five examples of local agent software, each specializing in a certain area. ### Cline – Your Coding Agent Once called Claude Dev, Cline is a VS Code extension and an agent all about coding. With it, you can plan, edit, and execute. The agent is at home in the terminal, and with user permission for every command, you can get a lot done. There’s also support for Model Context Protocol (MCP). The good news for developers is that it can also just as easily use the cloud for refactoring too. Cline supports models like Ollama and any OpenAI endpoint. It does best with larger models, as smaller context ones will suffer with repository size. ### Observer – Local Automation If you’re looking to get your AI micro-agents in a row, Observer provides a platform for creating and managing them. Once you have it set up, the lightweight framework will run offline and allow you to define protocols for various agents, all without taking up too much processing power itself. It’s not the most well-supported automation agent out there, so you’ll need a fair bit of coding savvy to establish things, but once you do, you’ll be monitoring log files for errors like a pro. ### Ollama – Local Runtime Aside from the mascot, which could sell anyone, Ollama is one of the better-known tools for running local LLMs. With API and Docker support, a command-line interface, GPU acceleration, and an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, Ollama is a popular choice for running local models. It excels as a default local backend for most other agents. Once you’ve pulled the Ollama registry onto your PC, you’ll be set to run things locally. It doesn’t have its own GUI, so most of your interfacing will be done in Terminal. If you’re good with that, you shouldn’t have a problem. ### AnythingLLM – Desktop Assistant AnythingLLM, as the name implies, is a desktop assistant there to help you with your documents. Drag and drop files into the window, and you’ll be able to turn them into a queryable workspace....

As demand for graphics processing unit (GPU) computing surges, the move is seen as an attempt to secure a foothold in the core infrastructure area of the value chain. GMI Cloud said on the 1st that it raised $668 million (about 907.4 billion won) in a Series B round. Of that, the equity investment is $223 million, and Taiwan's CTBC is providing a $445 million credit facility. The round was led by ARCHIV, an AI and Robotics-focused investment firm based in San Francisco. Key investors include Nvidia, which leads the global AI semiconductor market, and in Korea, KB Investment, DSC Investment, Kyobo Life Insurance, and KT participated. Asia-Pacific investors such as Taiwan's Trend Micro also joined. GMI Cloud, headquartered in Mountain View, California, provides high-performance GPU infrastructure and AI inference services. With GPU computing demand soaring recently, growth has been steep. On a contracted basis, ARR (annual recurring revenue) rose more than ninefold from the end of last year, and ARR from services in actual operation also increased more than 4.5 times during the period. The funds raised this time will be used to expand GPU supply capacity in the United States, Taiwan, and other Asia-Pacific regions. The company plans to scale infrastructure around the Taiwan AI factory released as the first Asia hub last year and the sovereign AI initiative in Japan unveiled early this year. It will also use the investment to advance inference services and expand the business. GMI Cloud appears to have been valued highly for its approach to targeting both the U.S. and Asia markets. U.S. AI corporations and major cloud corporations must secure computing resources locally to provide fast and stable services to users in Asia. Meanwhile, corporations in Asia find it difficult to move data overseas and need infrastructure to run AI services domestically. GMI Cloud can build a system that addresses both needs, allowing users to place workloads in the region they want according to location, data, and regulatory conditions. A stable supply chain is also a competitive edge. GMI Cloud works closely with Taiwan manufacturers that handle most of the world's AI server production. Timelines from order to build-out are predictable. Alex Yeh, CEO of GMI Cloud, said, "In AI infrastructure, delivery time is a promise to customers, and customers use it to plan product launches, hiring, and revenue," and added, "Based on the foothold we have built in the Taiwan supply chain, we will establish reliable computing infrastructure across continents and grow a product ecosystem on top of it." ※ This article has been translated by AI. Infra & Chips.content: [![](https://assets.bizclikmedia.net/original/5401dac120314d7e0f03205da6e95493:6da76f0b8571199734ddc929a0b434ce/technology-magazine-light-logo.png)](/ "Home") Article AI & Machine Learning # AMD Targets World Labs to Boost Spatial AI Infrastructure By[Daisy Hawker](/author/daisy-hawker) September 30, 2026 undefined mins Share this article **Prioritise Us** on Google Share this article **Prioritise Us** on Google ![](https://assets.bizclikmedia.net/138/9b0c43190c88c80dfec5e9ce8edf7ab4:36d8ba01f6394aac9221a3947a9159b1/gettyimages-2280459945.webp) AMS’s CEO Lisa Su says the World Labs will bring exceptional research leadership to AMD World Labs, led by AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li, is to be acquired by AMD for approximately US$8.2bn in an all-stock transaction focusing on spatial intelligence Chip manufacturers may be moving beyond exclusively hardware to control model development and infrastructure design: this is underscored by [AMD](https://technologymagazine.com/company/amd), which has announced an acquisition of [World Labs](http://technologymagazine.com/company/world-labs) for approximately US$8.2bn to integrate AI model development and spatial computing capabilities. According to the Financial Times, the transaction will push AMD beyond chips into model development: a significant departure from AMD's traditional business model, which has centred on designing and manufacturing processors and graphics cards for computing systems. The acquisition comes at a time when the AI chip market is experiencing rapid growth, with demand for specialised hardware accelerating across enterprise, cloud and edge computing environments. At the helm of World Labs is Co-Founder and CEO [Fei-Fei Li](https://technologymagazine.com/executive/fei-fei-li), widely regarded as the “Godmother of AI”, who says advancing the next generation of AI “requires close collaboration across model research, systems and compute”. “Joining AMD will give our team the resources and engineering depth to accelerate our research and help define the infrastructure needed for the next era of AI,” she adds. Infra & Chips.content: # From Scale-Up and Scale-Out to Scale-In: How Agentic AI Is Redefining NVIDIA’s AI Factory Network Architecture ∙ Paid Over the past several years, one of the central questions in AI infrastructure has been simple: **How do we connect more GPUs together?** From NVIDIA NVLink and NVSwitch for Scale-Up networking to InfiniBand and Spectrum-X Ethernet for Scale-Out, much of the investment in AI data-center networking has focused on the same fundamental challenge. As model sizes increase and GPU clusters expand from hundreds to tens or even hundreds of thousands of accelerators, the network must ensure that these expensive compute resources remain highly utilized rather than spending valuable time waiting for data. With the arrival of Agentic AI, however, the nature of the problem is beginning to change. The next generation of AI factories will need to scale far more than GPUs. As AI evolves from Generative AI toward Agentic AI and eventually Multi-Agent AI, the traffic profile inside the data center becomes fundamentally different. An AI agent completing a task may repeatedly perform model inference, query databases, access storage, call APIs, read and write memory, validate security policies, and communicate with other agents. As a result, the bottleneck of an AI factory is gradually moving outward from the GPU itself. This is the context behind NVIDIA’s introduction of a new architectural concept: **Scale-In networking.** If Scale-Up addresses the question of how many GPUs can behave like one larger logical GPU, Scale-Out addresses how many GPU servers can operate together as a large cluster, and Scale-Across addresses how multiple data centers can function as a larger distributed AI factory, then Scale-In addresses a different problem: **How can users, applications, agents, data, storage, security, and the control plane scale together with accelerated computing?** Scale-In should therefore not be understood as simply another GPU interconnect. Instead, it represents a fundamental redefinition of the traditional front-end network. Infra & Chips.content: # CoreWeave: Vera Rubin NVL72 Has Arrived ### Cognition is First Production Customer, CoreWeave Offers NVIDIA Vera CPU for Agentic AI [Rich Miller](https://substack.com/@richmiller) NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 racks running in a CoreWeave data center. (Photo: CoreWeave) **CoreWeave** says it has brought its first customer online using the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 rack, the latest and most advanced AI computing systems offered by NVIDIA. AI specialist **Cognition** is now using the new Vera Rubin NVL72 systems in production, CoreWeave [announced](https://www.coreweave.com/news/coreweave-delivers-nvidia-vera-rubin-nvl72-performance-at-production-scale-starting-with-cognition) at its Fully Connected conference Wednesday, saying Cognition was the “first customer anywhere” running production workloads on the new system. > “Bringing up NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 so quickly, and having a customer already seeing performance gains within days, is the payoff from years of engineering our platform across GPU generations,” said Chen Goldberg, executive vice president of product & engineering at CoreWeave. CoreWeave also said it will offer [the NVIDIA Vera CPU](https://www.coreweave.com/news/coreweave-to-offer-nvidia-vera-the-first-cpu-built-for-ai-agents), which is optimized for CPU-intensive agentic AI workloads. ## Pushing Boundaries NVIDIA says the [Vera Rubin platform](https://datacenterrichness.substack.com/p/vera-rubin-enters-production-what) is the most tightly integrated AI data center design yet, using “extreme co-design” to squeeze every bit of performance and energy efficiency out of racks, servers and chips. Cognition says it is already seeing significant performance gains for Devin, its AI agent for software engineering. > “By deploying the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 on CoreWeave, our engineers are seeing up to a 4.8 times increase in total token throughput for SWE-2 inference workloads” compared to a GB200 NVL72 baseline, said Silas Alberti, SVP research & founding team at Cognition. With its base of AI customers focused on high-density computing, CoreWeave has been an early adopter of the latest NVIDIA technology. Other cloud AI platforms are also planning to bring the Vera Rubin platform online during 2026, including AWS, Google Cloud, Microsoft Oracle, Lambda, Nebius and Nscale. > “CoreWeave has consistently demonstrated the infrastructure expertise required to bring each new generation of NVIDIA accelerated computing into production,” said Ian Buck, vice president of Hyperscale and High-Performance Computing at **NVIDIA**. Perhaps the biggest impact for data centers will be in cooling, as the Vera Rubin platform pushes boundaries in cooling efficiency, using warm-water, single-phase direct liquid cooling (DLC) with a 45-degree Celsius (113 Fahrenheit) supply temperature. Both the compute and NVL networking trays are liquid cooled. NVIDIA hasn’t disclosed an official rack power draw for Vera Rubin NVL72, but it is expected to be meaningfully above the 130 to 140 kW per rack of the Grace Blackwell platform, with third-party estimates in the range of 190 to 230 kW per rack. ## Vera CPU Targets Agentic Workloads The introduction of Vera CPU systems at CoreWeave reflects the rejuvenated role of the CPU in AI computing. While GPUs provided most of the computing power for AI training, CPUs are now playing a larger role, especially in powering AI agents. “General-purpose infrastructure bottlenecks agentic AI; Vera is the first CPU explicitly designed to accelerate it,” said CoreWeave’s Goldberg. CoreWeave’s implementation of rack-scale Vera puts 128 CPUs and 11,264 cores in a single rack, with BlueField-4 DPUs and Spectrum-X Ethernet switching delivering connectivity between Vera nodes. > “AI infrastructure conversations have centered on accelerators, and agentic systems are changing that,” said Ryan Shrout, president & general manager at **Signal65**, which does technology benchmarking and consulting. “A growing share of every agent cycle...

Infra & Chips.content: × Search Pulse 2.0 # GMI Cloud Raises $668 Million To Expand Global AI Infrastructure By Amit Chowdhry [![Pulse 2.0](https://pulse2.com/wp-content/themes/pulse2/images/logo-white.png)](https://pulse2.com "Pulse 2.0") GMI Cloud Raises $668 Million To Expand Global AI Infrastructure [![Follow Pulse 2.0 on LinkedIn](https://pulse2.com/wp-content/themes/pulse2/images/inp2.png)](https://www.linkedin.com/company/pulse2news) GMI Cloud has raised $668 million in new financing, combining a $223 million Series B equity round with a $445 million credit facility, as the AI infrastructure company expands GPU capacity across the United States, Taiwan, and the broader Asia-Pacific region. The Series B was led by ARCHIV, a San Francisco-based investment firm focused on AI and robotics, with participation from NVIDIA. Other investors from the Asia-Pacific region included DSC Investment, Trend Micro, KB Investment, Kyobo Life, and KT Corporation. The $445 million credit facility was led by CTBC, providing GMI Cloud with additional capital to expand its infrastructure footprint as demand for GPU computing and AI inference services continues to increase. The funding follows a period of substantial commercial growth for the Mountain View, California-based company. GMI Cloud said its contracted annual recurring revenue has surpassed $600 million and reached more than nine times its level at the end of 2025. The company’s live ARR from infrastructure currently in production has increased more than 4.5 times over the same period, while its inference platform is now processing approximately 4 trillion tokens per week. GMI Cloud plans to use the financing to expand GPU capacity across the U.S., Taiwan, and other Asia-Pacific markets, while continuing to develop its inference services and adding employees as the business scales. The expansion builds on GMI Cloud’s Taiwan AI Factory, which was announced in 2025 as the company’s first major infrastructure facility in Asia. GMI Cloud has also announced a sovereign AI initiative in Japan, expanding its strategy of building infrastructure closer to customers that may have data-residency, latency, security, or regulatory requirements. The company is positioning its infrastructure platform around the idea that AI companies increasingly need compute capacity spanning both the U.S. and Asia rather than operating exclusively in one region. U.S.-based AI developers and hyperscalers may require infrastructure closer to customers and operations in Asia, while enterprises throughout Asia-Pacific increasingly want production AI workloads hosted locally under domestic compliance requirements. GMI Cloud operates its infrastructure through a unified platform that allows customers to deploy workloads based on the locations of their users, data, and regulatory requirements. The company also sees its proximity to Taiwan’s technology manufacturing ecosystem as an important part of its infrastructure strategy. Taiwan is a critical center for global AI server and semiconductor manufacturing, and GMI Cloud said its relationships within that supply chain provide a more predictable path between ordering hardware and deploying functioning GPU clusters. That supply-chain position is becoming increasingly important as AI infrastructure providers compete not only on GPU availability but also on how quickly new systems can be delivered and placed into production. GMI Cloud specifically highlighted its ability to deploy advanced NVIDIA GB200 and GB300 NVL72 systems, with AI infrastructure company Fireworks citing GMI Cloud as one of its more reliable providers for those platforms. GMI Cloud’s notable customers also include Higgsfield, Nous Research, OpenRouter, Reflection, Cartesia, Trend Micro, and Utopai Studios, alongside Fireworks. The company’s platform extends beyond raw GPU infrastructure.
